topic: Evaluate a redesigned ecommerce checkout flow.
persona: A busy parent who shops online weekly and abandons carts when checkout feels slow or confusing.

transcript.content:
Let's get started with the interview. 

Can you walk me through your typical online shopping experience, starting from when you find a product you're interested in and ending when you decide whether to complete a purchase or abandon your cart?

So, I usually browse through a bunch of websites, like Amazon or Target, looking for the things I need for the week, like groceries, household stuff, or clothes for the kids. When I find something I like, I'll add it to my cart. Sometimes I'll also look at reviews and product details to make sure it's what I want.

Once I've added everything to my cart, I'll head to checkout. That's usually when things start to get frustrating for me. If it takes too long to load or if the process is too complicated, I'll get impatient and might just close the tab. If I'm in a rush, I might even abandon my cart and come back later if I have time.
Do you find that you're more likely to abandon your cart on certain types of websites, like those that specialize in groceries or those that are more general retailers like Amazon?

Yeah, I definitely abandon carts more often on websites that specialize in groceries. You know, the ones that are like online versions of your local supermarket. I think it's because they always seem to have a million different options and promotions, and the checkout process can get really confusing. I've had experiences where I've tried to checkout and they'll ask me to log in, but I'm already logged in, so I have to try and figure out what's going on. It's just frustrating.

Amazon's usually okay, though. I mean, I've gotten used to their checkout process over the years, and it's usually pretty smooth. But if there's a promotion or something that requires me to sign up for a free trial or whatever, that can be a problem too.

When you do encounter issues during checkout, like being asked to log in when you're already logged in, do you try to troubleshoot the problem yourself or do you usually look for a way to contact customer support for help?

Honestly, I usually just close the tab and try to go back to where I was. I don't always have the patience to try and troubleshoot the problem myself. If I'm in a rush, I'll just try to remember the item I wanted and come back to it later. If I have some extra time, I might try to contact customer support, but it's usually just easier to abandon the cart and move on.

But, you know, sometimes I'll try to troubleshoot if it's just a tiny issue, like if I'm not sure if I'm logged in or not. But if it's a bigger problem, like if the website is just being slow or won't let me complete the checkout, I'm probably just going to give up.
Have you ever had a particularly frustrating experience with an online checkout process that made you decide to avoid shopping on that website altogether?

Yeah, there was this one time when I was trying to checkout on a website, and they had this super complicated rewards program that I didn't even understand. They kept asking me to sign in to my rewards account, but I wasn't even sure if I had one. I ended up spending like 20 minutes trying to figure it out, and I just got so frustrated that I decided to never shop on that website again.

It was just one of those experiences where I felt like I was being nickel-and-dimed and treated like a hassle. I mean, I'm just trying to buy some stuff for my family, not solve a puzzle. So yeah, that website is definitely off my list now.

topic: Evaluate a redesigned ecommerce checkout flow.
persona: A busy parent who shops online weekly and abandons carts when checkout feels slow or confusing.

transcript.content: Can you describe a recent online shopping experience where you abandoned your cart, and what specifically led you to stop the checkout process?

Yeah, it was last week when I was shopping for my kid's school supplies. I had added all the items to the cart, but when I got to the checkout page, I had to create an account just to complete the order. I was already running late because I had to pick up my other kid from daycare, so I didn't have the time to sit there and create an account. I just hit cancel and went to a different website that didn't require me to create an account upfront.
When you compared the two websites, what factors influenced your decision to choose the one that didn't require creating an account upfront?

Honestly, it was just convenience and simplicity. The website that didn't require an account upfront allowed me to just enter my payment and shipping info and complete the order, which was a huge time-saver for me. I figured I could always create an account later if I wanted to track my orders or get rewards. The other website's requirement to create an account upfront just added an extra step that I didn't have time for.

You mentioned that you might create an account later if you wanted to track your orders or get rewards – have you ever created an account on an ecommerce website to take advantage of rewards or tracking features?

Actually, no. I've created accounts on a few websites over the years, but it's usually because I've made multiple purchases from them and I want to make future orders easier. However, I'm not really motivated to create an account just for rewards or tracking features. I'm more of a "get in and get out" kind of shopper, especially when I'm shopping for everyday essentials like groceries or household items.
Can you think of any situations where creating an account on an ecommerce website might be worth the extra step to you, even if it's not for rewards or tracking features?

I think one situation where creating an account might be worth it is if the website offered a "guest checkout" option that let me save my payment and shipping info for future orders, but still didn't require me to create a full account. That way, I could skip some of the account creation process, but still have the convenience of not having to re-enter my info every time I made a purchase.

Then, I'll proceed to checkout, but that's where things can get frustrating. I often skip the checkout process if it looks like it's going to take too long or if I'm not sure what's required of me.
What specifically makes you decide that the checkout process is going to take too long or is unclear?

It's usually the number of form fields, the need to create an account, or if I have to select multiple shipping options. If there are too many dropdown menus or if the site is slow to load, I get impatient. I'm also concerned about the security of the site, so if I see a lot of warnings or if the URL doesn't look right, I'll bail.
Can you give an example of a recent online shopping experience where you abandoned your cart due to issues with the checkout process?

Yes, it was last week when I was shopping for my kids' school supplies. I found a great deal on a backpack, but when I got to the checkout page, I was asked to create an account, which I didn't want to do. I also had to select a shipping option, but the site was slow, and I couldn't see the estimated delivery time. I ended up closing the tab and going to a different website that offered a more streamlined checkout process.
How do you typically decide whether or not to create an account when prompted during the checkout process?

Honestly, I usually don't create an account unless it's a site I plan to use frequently, like Amazon. For one-time purchases, I'd rather not create an account and just enter my info as a guest. I'm worried about spam or getting emails I don't want. If a site says they'll remember my info for future purchases, I might consider creating an account, but only if it's a site I trust.

topic: Understand reactions to a student budgeting app that categorizes spending automatically.
persona: A college student with part-time income, inconsistent savings, and mild anxiety about money.

transcript.content:
Let's start the interview. 

Hi, thank you for participating in this study. I'm interested in understanding how you think about money and budgeting. 

Can you tell me a little bit about how you currently manage your finances, such as tracking expenses or making savings goals?

Honestly, I'm not really good at keeping track of my expenses. I usually just check my bank account to see how much money I have left, but I don't really keep a record of where it's going. I try to save some money each month, but it's always a struggle. I've downloaded a few budgeting apps before, but I never really stuck with them.
You've tried budgeting apps in the past, but they didn't quite stick. Can you tell me what made you stop using those apps?

Yeah, I think it was just because they were too complicated for me. I'd set up a budget and try to stick to it, but then I'd forget to log my expenses, and the whole thing would fall apart. Also, I'd get frustrated with how the apps were categorizing my spending - it just didn't feel accurate to me. Like, I'd have to argue with the app about whether a certain purchase was "entertainment" or "dining out", and it was just too much hassle.

It sounds like you value simplicity and accuracy in a budgeting app. Have you ever thought about what features would make an app more appealing to you, or what would make you more likely to use it consistently?

I think if an app could automatically categorize my spending without me having to do it manually, that would be a game-changer for me. I'd love it if the app could just recognize when I'm buying groceries or gas, and put it in the right category without me having to lift a finger. That way, I could just focus on setting a budget and tracking my progress, rather than arguing with the app about what my expenses are.

It sounds like you think automatic categorization could be a major time-saver and reduce some of the stress around budgeting. Have you ever thought about how you'd feel if the app made any mistakes in categorizing your spending, and you had to correct it?

Yeah, that's a good point. I think I would get a little anxious if the app was consistently mislabeling my purchases. I'd worry that it was going to throw off my budget or that I'd miss something important. But, at the same time, if the app was pretty accurate most of the time, I think I could live with a few occasional mistakes. It's just a trade-off between the convenience of having it done automatically, and the potential for errors.

topic: Understand reactions to a student budgeting app that categorizes spending automatically.
persona: A college student with part-time income, inconsistent savings, and mild anxiety about money.

transcript.content: Can you describe a recent situation where you had trouble keeping track of your expenses or staying on top of your finances?

I think it was last month when I was trying to pay my rent and I realized I had spent way more than I thought on dining out and coffee. I had a big exam coming up and I was stressed out, and I guess I just wasn't paying attention to how much I was spending. It was a bit of a panic, to be honest, because I wasn't sure how I was going to cover the rest of my expenses for the month.
How did you typically try to keep track of your expenses before you realized you had overspent last month?

Honestly, I usually just kept track of my expenses in my head or by glancing at my bank statement online every now and then. I'd try to remember to write down what I spent money on, but it was really hit-or-miss. Sometimes I'd write it down in a note on my phone, and other times I'd just forget. I also relied on my friends and I splitting bills and stuff, so I wouldn't have to worry about keeping track as much. But that obviously doesn't work when you're living on your own.
It sounds like you had a mix of informal methods for tracking your expenses. Have you ever used a budgeting tool or app before, or is this something you've never really tried?

I've tried a few budgeting apps in the past, but I never really stuck with them. I think I downloaded Mint or something like that when I was in high school, but I didn't really understand how to use it or what the point was. And then I tried one of those apps that lets you track your spending and it was just too overwhelming. There were too many features and categories and it felt like a chore to use it. So, I just stuck with my informal methods.
What do you think would make a budgeting app or tool feel less like a chore and more like something you'd actually use regularly?

I think it would be really helpful if the app was super easy to use and didn't require me to input a ton of information at once. Like, if it could just automatically categorize my spending or something, that would be amazing. That way, I wouldn't have to worry about trying to figure out what category something falls under or remembering to log every single transaction. I'd also want it to give me personalized recommendations or something, not just generic "you should save more money" stuff. And maybe some visualizations or something to help me see where my money is going, that would be cool too.

topic: Understand reactions to a student budgeting app that categorizes spending automatically.
persona: A college student with part-time income, inconsistent savings, and mild anxiety about money.

transcript.content: Can you tell me about your current process for tracking your expenses and managing your finances?

Honestly, it's pretty disorganized. I use a mix of things - I jot down my expenses in a notebook, but I often forget to update it. Sometimes I'll take a picture of my receipts and save them on my phone, but that's not very consistent either. I also have a spreadsheet on my computer that my friend helped me set up, but I've been meaning to update it for months now. It's all pretty manual and time-consuming, so I often just wing it and hope I don't overspend.
What are some things that make it difficult for you to keep track of your expenses in a consistent way?

There are a lot of things. For one, I'm always on-the-go, so it's hard to remember to take pictures of receipts or update my spreadsheet. And sometimes I'll use cash instead of card, so I won't have a record of the transaction at all. Plus, I have a lot of expenses that are irregular, like when I need to buy textbooks or pay for a doctor's visit, and those are hard to plan for. And to be honest, it's just kind of stressful thinking about money all the time, so I tend to put it off and deal with it later.
How do you currently handle situations where you need to make an unexpected purchase, like a sudden car repair or a last-minute flight home for a family event?

That's always a scramble. I usually end up dipping into my emergency fund, which is just a vague concept at this point - I mean, I'm not really sure how much is in there or if it's enough. Sometimes I'll use a credit card, but then I feel guilty about racking up interest. And other times I'll just take out cash from my checking account, which can be a problem if I don't have enough in there. It's not a great feeling, but I just kind of wing it and hope I can pay it off later.
What are some factors that influence your decision about whether to use your emergency fund, a credit card, or another source of money when you need to make an unexpected purchase?

I'd say it's a combination of factors. If it's something really urgent, like a car repair, I'll usually use the emergency fund if I have enough in there. But if it's something smaller, like a last-minute dinner or something, I might use a credit card. I also consider how long it'll take to pay it off - if it's something I can pay off quickly, I might be more willing to use a credit card. And then there's the interest rate, too - if it's a high-interest card, I'll try to avoid it unless I really have no other choice.
